subject: Is there a way of manipulating ggplot scale breaks and labels?

messages.author: 99a1cfc66539313c
messages.subject: Is there a way of manipulating ggplot scale breaks and labels?
parts:
(Cross-posted from StackOverflow
http://stackoverflow.com/questions/5380417/is-there-a-way-of-manipulating-ggplot-scale-breaks-and-labels)

ggplot generally does a good job of creating sensible breaks and
labels in scales.

However, I find that in plot with many facets and perhaps a formatter=
statement, the labels tend to get too "dense" and overprint, for
example in this picture:

df <- data.frame(
fac=rep(LETTERS[1:10], 100),
x=rnorm(1000)
)

ggplot(df, aes(x=x)) +
geom_bar(binwidth=0.5) +
facet_grid(~fac) +
scale_x_continuous(formatter="percent")


I know that I can specify the breaks and labels of scales explicitly,
by providing breaks= and scale= arguments to scale_x_continuous.

However, I am processing survey data with many questions and a dozen
crossbreaks, so need to find a way to do this automatically.

Is there a way of telling ggplot to calculate breaks and labels
automatically, but just have fewer, say at the minimum, maximum and
zero point?

EDIT: Ideally, I don't want to specify the minimum and maximum points,
but somehow tap into the built-in ggplot training of scales, and use
the default calculated scale limits.

messages.subject: Re: Is there a way of manipulating ggplot scale breaks and labels?
parts:
I've had similar issues before and I ended up using if/else statements to set the font size based upon how many facets I had. Angling text also helps. 

Brandon

Hi,

Just a thought, it might be convenient to have a customizable
grid.pretty() function for use in ggplot2. Playing with its
parameters, or even defining a brand new one, would provide more
flexibility. All it would require would be the use of a different
alias in ggplot2's code, with default to grid::grid.pretty().

baptiste

messages.subject: Re: Is there a way of manipulating ggplot scale breaks and labels?
parts:
Brandon

Thank you. As a short term fix, I have done exactly what you
suggested - reducing font size and changing angle of text by 90
degrees. I also manually specified break points for the most
problematic plots.

In a separate forum, Hadley indicated that a future release of ggplot
will have finer-grained control of the scale breaks and ticks.

Andrie
